speech.text: Hurricane Elena makes landfall on Mexico's Yucatán coast.
Panama Canal reopens after a day-long closure.
Wildfire near Marseille forces thousands to evacuate.
Good afternoon, and welcome to World now.
I'm Paco Pixel, with Lola Byte.
Hurricane Elena has made landfall near Cancún with winds of one hundred and eighty kilometres per hour, according to Pixelburg Post.
Mexico's civil protection agency says about one point two million homes are without power and forty thousand people have gone to shelters.
Vic Vector, at our Americas desk, has the detail.
This is a life-threatening situation, the agency said.
The storm weakened slightly as it moved inland over the Yucatán peninsula.
Airports in Cancún and Mérida have closed, and hotels have moved guests to inner rooms.
Vic, what happens next?
Forecasters expect heavy rain over the next two days, with a risk of flooding in low areas.
Vic Vector, thank you.
The Panama Canal has reopened to ships after fog closed it for a day, Ledger Line reports.
The canal authority says about thirty ships are waiting to cross.
Shipping companies say the delays should clear within days.
Thick fog had forced the canal authority to stop all crossings, a rare step for the waterway.
Ships began moving again at dawn, with pilots guiding the first vessels through the locks at reduced speed.
Firefighters are battling a wildfire on a pine ridge north of Marseille.
Officials have asked people nearby to keep their windows closed because of the smoke.
About three thousand residents have been moved from three villages, local officials say, and a motorway has been closed.
Water-bombing planes are flying over the ridge, according to Bitport Herald.
The fire spread quickly in strong winds during the afternoon.
In Iceland, a fissure eruption has started again on the Reykjanes peninsula.
Scientists say lava is flowing away from nearby towns and flights are not affected.
It is the latest in a series of eruptions in the area since twenty twenty-one.
The fissure is about three kilometres long, according to the meteorological office.
A nearby spa has closed as a precaution, Pixelburg Post reports.
Heavy monsoon rain has flooded streets in several coastal towns in Kerala, India.
Officials have asked people to avoid travel where roads are under water.
Our Asia-Pacific correspondent Mika Voxel has more.
Local authorities have opened one hundred twenty relief camps and closed schools for two days.
Rain fell for most of the night, and water rose quickly in low-lying streets near the coast.
Boats were used to help people reach dry ground in some neighbourhoods.
Mika, what comes next?
Forecasters expect more heavy rain over the next three days.
Mika, thank you.
Norway's central bank has unexpectedly raised its main interest rate to four point seven five percent.
Most economists had expected no change, according to Bitport Herald.
Mortgage rates are expected to follow within weeks.
The rise is the bank's first move in more than a year.
The Norwegian krone strengthened after the announcement.
And one detail worth adding: the central bank said prices are rising faster than it expected.
Still to come: coral recovers on parts of the Great Barrier Reef off Queensland.
Our number of the day: forty thousand.
Lisbon has opened a new tram line along the Tagus river, Pixelburg Post reports.
The city says the nine kilometre route will carry forty thousand passengers a day and cut car traffic in the old town.
As the mayor put it: This line will change how people move around the old town.
Thanks, Paco.
A carmaker says it will close its plant near Turin by the end of next year.
Unions say two thousand four hundred jobs are at risk.
Now, around the world.
In Kenya, a solar farm north of Nairobi has started supplying power to the national grid.
Now to the Andes.
Archaeologists in Peru say they have found the remains of a temple about three thousand years old in the northern Andes.
Rail operators in Japan say their bullet trains ran with an average delay of under one minute last year.
The city of Paris has announced plans to plant one hundred seventy thousand trees by twenty thirty to cool the city in summer.
Now to the Greek islands.
Strong winds have forced ferry operators to cancel sailings between Athens and several Greek islands, according to Pixelburg Post.
And finally: scientists say coral cover has grown on parts of the Great Barrier Reef for a second year.
The reef is showing it can bounce back when it gets a break, a lead researcher said.
Researchers warn that another hot summer could undo the gains, Bitport Herald reports.
The measurements come from surveys of more than a hundred reefs along the coast of Queensland.
Scientists say fast-growing corals have recovered quickest.
There is hope for us yet.
Let us not get carried away.
That's World now.
From Lola Byte and from me, thank you for watching.
Stay with us on Globit twenty-four.
